title: The Pythagorean comma
hook: Twelve perfect fifths overshoot seven octaves, so pianos are tuned slightly off.
peek: Climb twelve perfect fifths from a note and you should land exactly seven octaves higher. You do not. You overshoot by a sliver called the Pythagorean comma, and modern pianos hide it by making every fifth very slightly impure.
lede: A perfect fifth is the sweetest interval after the octave: two notes whose frequencies sit in a ratio of 3 to 2. Stack twelve of them, from C through every note, and you should arrive back at C, seven octaves up. The arithmetic says otherwise. You land about a quarter of a semitone too high, and this tiny gap has shaped tuning for centuries.

bullets.text: Twelve fifths multiply out to 1.5 to the twelfth power, about 129.7. Seven octaves are 2 to the seventh, exactly 128. The ratio between them, roughly 1.0136, is the Pythagorean comma.
Tuners using pure fifths had to dump the leftover gap somewhere. One fifth ended up badly out of tune, a harsh interval nicknamed the wolf, and musicians simply avoided keys that used it.

Modern pianos share the comma out evenly. Each fifth is narrowed by about one fiftieth of a semitone, too small for most ears to notice, so every key sounds equally good and none sounds perfectly pure.
Because tempered fifths are not quite pure, two notes played together make a slow pulse, called beating. Tuners listen for it and set each fifth to beat at a steady, gentle rate.
